question: Where do path-scoped rule files live in a Claude Code project?

explanations: Correct — `.claude/rules/` is the project-scoped directory for path-conditional rule files, version-controlled with the repo.

`CLAUDE.md` is a memory file, not a container for path-scoped rule definitions.

question: Which YAML frontmatter field in a `.claude/rules/` file declares which files the rule applies to?

question: When does a `.claude/rules/` file with `paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]` enter Claude's context?

On every interaction in the project, the same way `CLAUDE.md` does

Activation is keyed to the file Claude is currently editing, not the mere presence of matching files in the repo.

question: Which glob pattern matches every React test file anywhere in the repo, including deeply nested directories?

`**/*.test.tsx`

question: Tests are colocated next to source files (`Button.test.tsx` next to `Button.tsx`) throughout the repo. Which mechanism best applies test-only conventions without affecting non-test edits?
options: A `.claude/rules/` file with `paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]`

Adding the conventions to the root `CLAUDE.md` under a `## Tests` heading
A `.claude/skills/test-conventions/SKILL.md`
explanations: Correct — globs match files by shape regardless of directory, and the rule only activates when a test file is being edited.
A directory `CLAUDE.md` applies to every file in that directory, polluting non-test edits with test conventions.
Always-loaded; relies on Claude inferring which section applies, and tests-spread-across-tree means no clean directory boundary.

question: What is the correct YAML form for the `paths` frontmatter field?

question: How does a directory-level `CLAUDE.md` differ from a path-scoped rule in terms of when it loads?
options: Both load only when a matching file is opened

Correct — `CLAUDE.md` is always-loaded in its scope; path-scoped rules are conditional on the edited file.
`CLAUDE.md` is scope-bound (project or subdirectory) and path rules are conditional — neither is unconditionally global.

question: Which is a primary token-budget benefit of path-scoped rules over a single large root `CLAUDE.md`?
options: Path-scoped rules are stored on disk only and never sent to the model
Path-scoped rules are compressed by the harness whereas `CLAUDE.md` is sent verbatim

Caching behaviour isn't the documented advantage; conditional loading is.

question: A team wants conventions for SQL migrations to apply regardless of which service folder a migration lives under. Which `paths` value fits best?

Matches all SQL files, including non-migrations; too broad and missing the `migrations/` segment.
Restricted to one specific layout; misses migrations elsewhere (e.g., `apps/foo/migrations/*.sql`).

question: What happens if you create a `.claude/rules/` file with no `paths` field at all?

It loads globally for every interaction (treat as always-on)

question: You want React-test conventions to apply to every test file in the repo, even though tests are colocated alongside source. Which is the correct configuration?
options: A `.claude/commands/test.md` slash command developers run before editing tests
A `tests/CLAUDE.md` file describing the conventions
A `.claude/rules/test.md` file with frontmatter `paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]`
An entry in the root `CLAUDE.md` under a `## Test conventions` heading
explanations: A slash command is user-triggered; it doesn't auto-apply when a test file is opened.
A subdirectory `CLAUDE.md` only covers files under `tests/`; it can't reach colocated tests elsewhere.

Always-loaded for every interaction; relies on Claude inferring which section applies on each edit.

question: Which YAML frontmatter snippet correctly scopes a rule to all test files in a TypeScript repo (both `.ts` and `.tsx`)?

question: A team adds a `frontend/CLAUDE.md` that describes both component layout AND test conventions. Devs notice Claude occasionally adds `describe` blocks while editing non-test component files. What's the better fix?
options: Move both the component layout and test conventions into the root `CLAUDE.md`
Tell Claude in the prompt to ignore the test conventions when editing components
Add a `# Important` section at the top of `frontend/CLAUDE.md` reminding Claude which section applies to which file

Adds more text without changing the load-time behaviour; the test conventions are still in context for every component edit.

question: You define a rule with `paths: ["*.test.tsx"]`. Tests at `apps/storefront/components/Button.test.tsx` aren't picking up the conventions. What's the most likely cause?

Skills require explicit invocation and are unrelated to automatic file-shape activation.
`paths` matches against files Claude is editing across the repo, not files in the rules directory.

question: Your repo has tests scattered across `apps/*/`, `packages/*/`, and `services/*/`. You want one set of test conventions everywhere. What's the most maintainable mechanism?

Duplicates the convention across many CLAUDE.md files; drifts over time and still doesn't reach colocated tests.
Always-loaded for every interaction and relies on inference for which section applies.
Slash commands are user-invoked, not automatic on file edit; impractical as a default convention enforcer.

question: Which is a legitimate reason to keep some context in a directory-level `CLAUDE.md` instead of converting everything to path-scoped rules?
options: Migration safety rules that apply only to `.sql` files

File-type-specific; a `paths: ["**/*.tf"]` rule scopes precisely.

question: Your team has separate conventions for tests, migrations, and Terraform. What's the recommended file organisation under `.claude/rules/`?

Rules aren't organised by repo directory; they're organised by file-shape concern.
Slash commands are user-triggered prompts, not automatic conventions tied to file edits.

question: When is a `.claude/rules/` file with no `paths` field appropriate?

question: Why is `**/*.test.tsx` preferred over `tests/**/*.tsx` for a path-scoped test rule in a repo where tests are colocated?

question: Which scenario most strongly indicates `.claude/rules/` with globs is the right tool over a `CLAUDE.md`?

question: A `.claude/rules/migrations.md` file sets `paths: ["**/migrations/*.sql"]`. The team starts placing migrations under `db/changes/` instead. Without updating the rule, what behaviour should you predict?

question: Why might a developer prefer a path-scoped rule over a subdirectory `CLAUDE.md` even when matching files all happen to live in one directory today?

question: A path-scoped rule and the root `CLAUDE.md` give slightly different guidance on a niche edge case. When Claude edits a matching file, what's the realistic expectation about how they interact?

question: A `.claude/rules/security-headers.md` enforces specific HTTP-header conventions for API handlers; it has `paths: ["apps/*/api/**/*.ts"]`. question: An engineer notices the test rule occasionally seems "already in effect" while Claude is reasoning about an unrelated component edit, even though the file being modified isn't a test. Which is the most likely real explanation?

question: A senior reviewer claims `.claude/rules/` is just "a more compact `CLAUDE.md`" and that any pattern of CLAUDE.md hierarchy could be re-expressed as a single global rule. Identify the most precise principle that pushes back on this framing.

question: A team has `paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]` and a separate `paths: ["apps/web/**/*"]` rule. While editing `apps/web/components/Button.test.tsx` they observe both rules' content in context. A teammate insists this is a bug and asks which rule "should win." What's the precise principle?

question: A team moves test conventions from the root `CLAUDE.md` into `.claude/rules/tests.md` (`paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]`). question: Faced with the choice between `frontend/CLAUDE.md` (covers everything in `frontend/`) and `.claude/rules/frontend-components.md` with `paths: ["frontend/**/*.{ts,tsx}"]`, which is the strongest reason to pick the path-scoped form even though every matching file is under `frontend/`?

question: A rule has `paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]`. A developer edits `Button.test.tsx.snap` (a Jest snapshot). The convention does not activate, and the developer files a bug. What's the correct explanation?
options: Globs implicitly match any extension after a dot
Snapshot files always activate the corresponding test rule by convention

Globs match against the full filename including extension; `**/*.test.tsx` does not match `*.test.tsx.snap` — the rule isn't broken, the glob simply doesn't cover that file. Add `**/*.test.tsx.snap` (or a broader pattern) if you want it to.
Path-scoped rules ignore extensions entirely and match on basename only
explanations: Globs do not implicitly accept arbitrary extension suffixes.
There is no documented "by convention" snapshot inclusion.
Correct — globs are literal up to wildcards; `.tsx` is a different extension than `.tsx.snap`, and you have to opt the latter in.
Globs match the full path, not just the basename.

question: Given (a) `frontend/CLAUDE.md` describing the React component architecture and (b) `.claude/rules/tests.md` with `paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]`, and Claude is asked to add a snapshot test next to `frontend/components/Modal.tsx`, which content is in context as Claude writes `Modal.test.tsx`?
options: Both — `frontend/CLAUDE.md` is always loaded for files under `frontend/`, and the test rule activates because the new file matches `**/*.test.tsx`
Only `frontend/CLAUDE.md` — path-scoped rules don't load for newly-created files until they're saved
Only the test rule — directory `CLAUDE.md` files are suppressed when a path-scoped rule activates
Neither — until the test passes, neither configuration is considered active
explanations: Correct — `CLAUDE.md` is always-on in scope; the path-rule activates because the file Claude is editing matches the glob; both contribute.
There is no documented "saved file" gate on activation.
There is no documented suppression of `CLAUDE.md` by activated rules; they coexist.
Activation isn't gated on test execution.

question: A team enforces fixture conventions via a `.claude/rules/fixtures.md` file with `paths: ["**/__fixtures__/**"]`. A developer asks: "why not just put it in the root `CLAUDE.md`? It's only ten lines." Which response captures the principled reason most precisely?
options: Path-scoped rules are mandatory for any file under a `__` prefixed directory
Ten-line conventions exceed the documented size threshold for `CLAUDE.md`
`CLAUDE.md` cannot describe fixture conventions; that's a `.claude/rules/`-only category

Always-loading those ten lines means they're in context for every interaction in the project, including unrelated production-code edits where they create noise; path-scoping injects them only when a fixture file is actually being touched
explanations: There is no documented requirement keyed to `__` prefixes.
There is no documented size threshold of that shape.
`CLAUDE.md` can describe any conventions; the question is whether always-loading them is appropriate.
Correct — the cost of "only ten lines" is paid on every interaction project-wide; conditional activation prevents unrelated edits from dragging in fixture-specific guidance.

question: A `.claude/rules/` file has frontmatter with `paths` omitted (no field). The author intends "only loads when a `*.md` file is edited" because the rule is itself a Markdown file. What's the precise correction?
options: The rule won't load at all because `paths` is required

Rule activation is keyed to the *edited* file's path matching `paths`, not to the rule file's own path; without `paths` the rule loads globally. Add `paths: ["**/*.md"]` if you want activation tied to Markdown edits.
The rule will activate when any other rule file is edited
The rule will activate only inside `.claude/rules/` editing sessions
explanations: Omitting `paths` doesn't disable the rule; it removes the constraint.
Correct — the field constrains the *target* file Claude is editing, not the rule's own filename; missing `paths` means "no constraint" i.e. global.
Activation isn't tied to other rule files being edited.
Activation isn't tied to the rules directory itself.
